CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION
1.1 BACKGROUND OF THE STUDY
Learning Management Systems (LMS) support the organization of course materials, academic
activities, and communication across different devices. International research shows that their
usefulness depends on how well the available functions meet learners’ needs. In Saudi Arabia, Alfalah
(2023) surveyed 258 students at Hail University, Aljouf University, and Northern Border University
about mobile LMS adoption. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and learning intention were
associated with intention to use the system. These findings connect access with students’ expectations
of useful and understandable academic functions, providing a broad basis for examining a multi-
platform learning environment.
Within computing education, an LMS also needs to support subject-specific activities and
purposeful participation. Ahmed et al. (2025) evaluated a gamified, mobile, cloud-based LMS with
60 second-year students taking Object-Oriented Programming at Mansoura University in Egypt. The
experimental group obtained higher post-test achievement and engagement scores than the
comparison group. Jaramillo-Mediavilla et al. (2024) reviewed gamification research and reported
favorable findings in parts of the literature, while identifying gaps in examining motivation and
academic performance together. These studies support considering programming and participation
tools within an LMS, although their educational results cannot be presumed for another institution.
In the Philippines, institutional studies connect LMS use with course organization and the
experience of completing academic tasks. Llamas et al. (2025) examined the Moodle-based LMS at
Mindanao State University–Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU–IIT) in Iligan City and identified
concerns in usability, communication, course building, monitoring and assessment, content
management, and technical support. Dela Rosa (2023) examined Canvas Free for Teachers with third-
year BSIT students at Bulacan State University, who evaluated its lesson modules and assessments
favorably. Together, these studies indicate that academic functions and user experiences must be
examined within their particular institutional and course settings.

At Colegio de Montalban, the present study focuses on the Institute of Computing Studies
(ICS), which offers the Bachelor of Science in Information Technology (BSIT) and Bachelor of
Science in Computer Engineering (BSCpE) programs. Its computing workflows involve course
resources, submissions, programming activities, assessment records, personal study, and faculty
coordination. The research group’s initial project description identifies the use of separate academic
and personal-organization tools as a concern. Local requirements gathering will establish the extent
of this fragmentation and the specific difficulties experienced by ICS students and instructors.
The development problem is how to connect these activities while maintaining clear
responsibilities and appropriate access to information. Students require understandable access to
approved coursework, personal grades, and study tools. Instructors require manageable teaching,
grading, and communication workflows. Academic oversight and administration require their own
restricted functions, particularly when course information, faculty responsibilities, schedules, and
calendar events are shared. These requirements call for a coordinated design that protects individual
academic records.
In response, the study proposes the CdM Learning Management System (CdM LMS) for ICS.
The Web Portal will serve as the principal academic environment, the Mobile Application will
support selected academic and productivity activities, and the native Desktop Application will
function as the Administrator Console. Shared backend workflows and a centralized database will
connect their applicable records. The researchers will develop and evaluate the system using role-
appropriate feedback from ICS students and instructors and researcher-conducted technical checks.
The study will provide evidence about the evaluated release’s software quality and workflow
suitability rather than assume improvements in grades or long-term learning outcomes.
1.2 STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM
This study seeks to determine the level of software quality of the LMS for ICS at Colegio de
Montalban in supporting coordinated academic resource and grade management, learning support,
academic coordination, and system administration. The evaluation will follow six selected

characteristics of the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Software Product Quality Model (International
Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2023).
Specifically, the study seeks to answer the following questions:
1. What is the evaluated software quality of CdM LMS in supporting academic resource and grade-
management workflows in terms of functional suitability, as measured by:
• Functional completeness in supporting course materials, assignments, dynamic grading, CodeLab
activities, Git-integrated submissions, and the defined academic coordination functions;
• Functional correctness of weighted grade computations, EXP and level calculations, descriptive
analytics, and schedule revisions and exceptions;
• Functional appropriateness in supporting connected academic workflows for BSIT and BSCpE
users within their assigned roles and platform responsibilities?
2. What is the evaluated software quality of CdM LMS in providing understandable and engaging
task interaction in terms of interaction capability, as reflected in:
• Appropriateness recognizability of course, grading, productivity, gamification, and academic
coordination functions;
• Learnability of permitted tasks in the Web Portal, selected Mobile Application functions, and
administrator-only Desktop Application;
• User engagement supported by EXP, levels, achievements, leaderboards, study tools, and the
moderated Knowledge Exchange environment?
3. What is the evaluated software quality of CdM LMS in protecting academic information and
controlling access in terms of security, as demonstrated by:
• Confidentiality of student grades, personal notes, academic records, and restricted course
information;

• Integrity of grades, submissions, schedule records, and events during authorized updates and
concurrent actions;
• Accountability through activity and audit records for designated administrative actions, academic
coordination changes, and Knowledge Exchange moderation?
4. What is the evaluated software quality of CdM LMS in processing academic information and
maintaining applicable shared records in terms of performance efficiency, as indicated by:
• Time behavior in computing grades, generating descriptive analytics and calendar views, retrieving
course resources, and displaying relevant in-LMS updates;
• Resource utilization during the processing and retrieval of shared information by the authorized
Web, Mobile, and Desktop components under defined workloads?
5. What is the evaluated software quality of CdM LMS in providing stable access to permitted
academic and study functions in terms of reliability, as evaluated through:
• Availability of the Web Portal, supported mobile study tools, and Administrator Console during the
defined evaluation period;
• Fault tolerance when processing interrupted requests, concurrent grade updates, or simultaneous
Knowledge Exchange activity, including the handling of failed operations without incomplete or
duplicate records?
6. What is the evaluated software quality of CdM LMS in supporting consistent information exchange
and operation alongside other software in terms of compatibility, as indicated by:
• Interoperability among the Web Portal, Mobile Application, and Administrator Console through
their applicable shared records and authorized backend workflows;
• Co-existence of the Administrator Console with other software in the supported administrator
workstation environment without adversely affecting their operation?

1.3 STATEMENT OF THE OBJECTIVES
1.3.1 General Objective
To develop and evaluate a Learning Management System for the Institute of Computing
Studies at Colegio de Montalban that coordinates academic management, learning support, academic
oversight, and system administration through shared information and role-appropriate access.
1.3.2 Specific Objectives
1. Establish shared backend services and a centralized PostgreSQL database for the principal Web
Portal, complementary Mobile Application, and administrator-only Desktop Application, with
credential-based authentication, account-status controls, and server-enforced access for Student,
Instructor, Super User, and Administrator roles.
2. Develop course and section management that allows authorized instructors to organize materials,
annotations, assignments, announcements, and deadlines, and allows enrolled students to access
resources and submit permitted work under the applicable validation rules.
3. Implement a Dynamic Gradebook with configurable assessment components and weights, score
recording, automatic weighted-grade computations, personal student grade views, instructor
performance summaries, and CSV grade export; verify computed values and charts against
documented test records.
4. Provide CodeLab for in-browser programming execution and assessment against predefined test
cases, and a separate Git-integrated workflow for repository-based coursework submission and
instructor review; verify the supported submission and access rules for each workflow.
5. Develop notes, task lists, flashcards, review and mastery records, focus timers, and study-session
tracking, together with rule-based EXP, levels, achievements, badges, streaks, and department
leaderboards; verify progression calculations and the separation of EXP from course grades and
forum reputation.

6. Implement Knowledge Exchange for academic questions, answers, and resource sharing, with
authorized instructor moderation, Faculty-Verified Answers, contribution-based reputation, and
records of designated moderation actions.
7. Develop the faculty directory and academic operations hub, distinguishing program affiliations and
Dean or Program Head designations from primary account roles, and providing restricted course
supervision that excludes student identities, individual grades, submissions, assessment attempts, and
answers.
8. Implement Asia/Manila-based weekly course schedules with effective-dated revision history and
future occurrence cancellation, rescheduling, and restoration; provide authorized calendar views,
audience-targeted saved events, coursework deadlines, and private note–event snapshot conversion,
and verify their visibility and preservation rules.
9. Provide the Administrator Console with account approval, status and role management, permitted
configuration, activity and audit records, reporting, and the backup and recovery functions supported
by the evaluated release; verify that administrative permissions remain separate from academic
oversight.
10. Evaluate the developed system in terms of functional suitability, interaction capability, security,
performance efficiency, reliability, and compatibility using role-appropriate tasks, feedback from
eligible ICS students and instructors, and technical checks conducted by the researchers, and
document defects and limitations identified in the evaluated version.

1.4 CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK
Figure 1
Conceptual framework of CdM LMS using IPO with feedback
The conceptual framework follows the Input–Process–Output (IPO) model with feedback, as
shown in Figure 1. It organizes the study’s requirements and resources, development and evaluation
activities, and expected system output. Purwanto et al. (2025) examined limitations of linear IPO
representations and proposed an IMOI adaptation in which outputs and feedback inform subsequent
iterations. The present study retains IPO while incorporating feedback into requirement refinement
and succeeding development cycles.

The Input component comprises related literature, initial academic practices and concerns
within ICS, and system requirements. The literature covers academic management, programming
coursework, learning support, and collaboration. Local requirements gathering will examine the use
of separate academic and productivity tools, resource management, faculty coordination, and access
conditions. These concerns will be investigated rather than reported as established local findings in
advance.
Technical inputs include development workstations, supported client devices, Next.js
services, PostgreSQL, web browsers, the Expo mobile application, and the Electron Administrator
Console. Connectivity, persistent storage, programming execution, repository access, authorization,
continuity arrangements, and test configurations will define the operating environment. Estimated
equipment specifications will be distinguished from configurations demonstrated during evaluation.
The Process component combines iterative development with requirements-based testing and
software-quality evaluation. Planning, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Review will
organize successive increments. The modules will address academic management, computing
coursework, personal study, gamification, collaboration, academic coordination, and administration.
Their availability will follow Student, Instructor, Super User, and Administrator permissions and the
complementary responsibilities of the three applications.
The evaluation will use six selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics: Functional
Suitability, Interaction Capability, Security, Performance Efficiency, Reliability, and Compatibility
(ISO, 2023). Respondent ratings will describe experiences with assigned tasks, while technical checks
will examine calculations, access restrictions, record handling, performance, and shared information.
Abid et al. (2024) provide a feature-based example of systematic LMS evaluation; the study’s quality
characteristics are derived from ISO/IEC 25010:2023.
The Output is the developed and evaluated CdM LMS release for ICS. It will provide a
principal Web Portal, selected mobile support, and a native Administrator Console around shared
records and authorized workflows. Feedback from testing, evaluation, and review will return to the

Input component to refine requirements and priorities. Revised inputs will guide subsequent
development cycles. Findings will concern the evaluated release and will not establish long-term
educational effects or institution-wide adoption.
1.5 OPERATIONAL FRAMEWORK
Figure 2
Adapted Agile development cycle for CdM LMS
The researchers will use an adapted Agile development approach consisting of Planning,
Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Review. Alsaqqa et al. (2020) describe Agile
values, iterative methods, and responsiveness to changing requirements. The six stages used here are
the project’s operational organization rather than a universal Agile sequence. Each cycle will address
prioritized requirements and produce an increment for examination and refinement.
Planning Phase. The researchers will gather local requirements from ICS students and
instructors. Llamas et al. (2025) identify LMS usability and workflow concerns, while Guico (2026)
highlights preparation, resource access, and training needs. These findings inform topics for local
investigation. Requirements will specify role responsibilities, platform coverage, expected behavior,
and acceptance criteria in a prioritized backlog.

Design Phase. Architecture, database relationships, workflows, and interfaces will be
prepared from the requirements. Flowcharts, ERDs, and DFDs will identify information movement
and component responsibilities. Attention to navigation and task feedback is supported by the user-
experience concerns examined by Laspiñas and Almerez (2024). The design will separate academic
supervision from teaching and administration and protect personal academic records.
Development Phase. Selected functions will be implemented incrementally using the Next.js
backend, PostgreSQL database, and applicable clients. Development will connect academic
management, programming coursework, study tools, gamification, collaboration, coordination, and
administration. Each increment will be checked against its acceptance criteria. The release record will
distinguish implemented, proposed, tested, and evaluation-enabled functions.
Testing Phase. Controlled accounts and datasets will be used to examine correctness,
authorization, integrity, integration, performance, and failure handling. The evaluation release will
also undergo role-appropriate task assessment aligned with the six selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023
characteristics (ISO, 2023). Technical results and respondent ratings will be reported separately.
Defects will be corrected and retested before affected functions are evaluated.
Deployment Phase. A reviewed release will be configured in a controlled environment. The
researchers will verify startup, backend connectivity, accounts, client builds, and available continuity
procedures. Participants will receive task guidance. The release version, enabled modules, device
configurations, and unresolved limitations will be recorded; controlled evaluation will not be
described as institution-wide deployment.
Review Phase. The researchers will examine their technical test records, questionnaire
responses, and task feedback from eligible ICS students and instructors. Findings will identify
supported behavior, defects, and refinement priorities. These priorities will return to the development
backlog, and corrected functions will undergo further testing.

1.6 SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS
The study covers the development and software-quality evaluation of CdM LMS for the
Institute of Computing Studies at Colegio de Montalban, including BSIT and BSCpE students,
instructors, and supporting academic and administrative workflows. Participation is not restricted to
one student year level. IBE and ITE configuration is a technical application capability; those institutes
are outside the research population and generalization of findings.
The Web Portal is the principal academic environment and the initial platform for the
coordination expansion. Mobile provides selected academic and productivity functions according to
the evaluated build. The native Desktop Application is the Administrator Console. Super User
oversight is web-based; native mobile parity for the expansion and native Super User console entry
are excluded. A role and platform matrix will identify the functions actually tested.
Functional coverage includes course resources and submissions, the Dynamic Gradebook,
descriptive analytics, separate CodeLab and Git coursework workflows, Knowledge Exchange,
personal notes and study tools, gamified progression, faculty organization, restricted supervision,
schedules, targeted events, and administration. Dean and Program Head are academic designations
attached to eligible accounts. They do not replace the four primary roles or automatically grant Super
User privileges.
Evaluation respondents will consist only of eligible ICS students and instructors with prior
LMS experience, selected through criterion-based purposive sampling. Participants must voluntarily
agree and perform relevant tasks before rating them. The researchers will conduct technical checks
using controlled accounts and datasets. Administrator and Super User functions remain within system
development and technical verification, but they will not form separate respondent groups. Instrument
review by the adviser and faculty validators is distinct from participation in the evaluation sample.
Operation depends on supported devices, connectivity, and service availability. The study
does not claim universal operating-system support, identical platform functions, uninterrupted
service, or full offline coursework. Hardware figures are estimates until tested. Programming

languages, repository access, reporting, and continuity coverage will be limited to the documented
evaluation release.
Academic analytics describe existing records. Rule-based attention indicators do not predict
future achievement. CodeLab checks predefined cases, while Git history supports review without
proving authorship or eliminating plagiarism. Tab switching, copy/paste, and fullscreen events are
contextual assessment indicators rather than conclusive cheating evidence. Optional grade incentives
will be evaluated only when their effect and institutional authorization are documented; EXP, forum
reputation, and academic grades remain distinct measures.
Scheduling uses Asia/Manila, selected weekdays, one shared time pair, date bounds, and
effective-dated revisions. Individual future classes may be cancelled, rescheduled, or restored.
Arbitrary recurrence, multiple weekly time patterns, automatic attendance, holiday cancellation,
room-conflict prevention, and timetable optimization are excluded. Student recurring timetable
projection is excluded; authorized events and coursework deadlines remain available.
Supervision excludes student identities, individual grades, submissions, attempts, answers,
and teaching controls. Event audiences govern LMS visibility without implying external delivery or
Google synchronization. Note–event conversion creates private snapshots; later edits do not
propagate. The descriptive study will not determine long-term changes in achievement, motivation,
employability, or study habits. Findings apply to the selected ICS participants, tasks, and evaluated
release.
1.7 SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY
The proposed CdM LMS may contribute to the Institute of Computing Studies (ICS) by
providing an integrated environment for managing academic and technical learning activities across
Web, Mobile, and Desktop platforms. The study may provide value to the following:
Institute of Computing Studies and Colegio de Montalban. The study may provide an
institutional basis for organizing related academic information and examining whether a tailored

LMS meets the needs of ICS. Its documented requirements and evaluation findings may support
decisions about further development, maintenance, and possible adoption.
Students. The system is intended to provide a coordinated place for accessing coursework and
feedback and managing personal study activities. Students may benefit from clearer access to their
own academic information and opportunities for moderated peer support. These expected benefits
remain distinct from measured improvements in academic achievement.
Instructors. The study may support more consistent handling of course resources,
submissions, grading records, programming activities, and academic communication. Evaluation
findings may identify interaction or workflow difficulties that require correction before broader use.
Super Users and Program Heads. Restricted Super User supervision may support authorized
academic oversight. Program Heads may benefit from faculty information and designation-specific
event publication. These responsibilities will remain distinct from teaching and system
administration.
Administrators. The dedicated console is intended to support controlled account operations,
system records, reporting, and supported continuity functions. Documenting access boundaries and
audit behavior may assist in maintaining accountability for administrative actions.
Future researchers and developers. The study may provide a reference for examining an
institutional LMS with complementary applications, computing-specific workflows, and limited
academic supervision. Its limitations and evaluation findings may also identify questions requiring
separate research, including longer-term educational outcomes and broader platform coverage.
1.8 GENERAL FEATURES OF THE SYSTEM / STUDY
CdM LMS comprises complementary applications connected through shared backend
services and a centralized database. The following groups describe intended feature coverage. A
release record will distinguish existing modules, planned extensions, tested functions, and functions
enabled for evaluation. Availability is governed by role and platform coverage.

Core Functional Features
Academic and Course Management
Authorized Instructors organize courses, sections, learning materials, annotations,
assignments, announcements, and deadlines. Students request enrollment using valid course codes;
access is granted after approval. Streams, classwork, people, and grades organize approved course
information and permitted records.
Grading and Academic Analytics
The Dynamic Gradebook supports configurable assessment components and weights, score
recording, computed grades, authorized personal grade views, descriptive charts, and permitted CSV
exports. Rule-based attention indicators summarize recorded conditions; they do not predict
achievement.
Programming and Collaborative Learning
CodeLab supports browser-based code execution and assessment against predefined test
cases. Git-integrated coursework supports a separate repository submission and Instructor review
workflow. Knowledge Exchange supports questions, answers, resources, authorized moderation,
Faculty-Verified Answers, and contribution reputation.
Personal Study and Gamification
Personal notes, tasks, flashcards, review and mastery records, focus timers, and study-session
records support organization and practice. Configured EXP, levels, achievements, badges, streaks,
and leaderboards describe eligible participation. EXP, academic grades, and forum reputation remain
distinct.
Academic Coordination and Calendar
The expansion will provide a faculty directory and organizational chart, a restricted academic
operations hub, safe course supervision, effective-dated weekly schedule revisions, future occurrence
exceptions, audience-targeted events, and private note–event snapshots. Day, Week, Month, and Year

views will combine permitted saved events, applicable generated classes, and coursework deadlines.
Student recurring timetable projection is outside the stated release.
User Features
Role-Based Workspaces
Students access approved coursework, personal grades, study tools, and permitted
collaboration. Instructors manage assigned teaching activities and related coordination. Super Users
perform restricted web-based academic oversight without grading or system administration.
Administrators use the native Console for protected account, configuration, audit, reporting, and
supported continuity operations. Dean and Program Head are academic designations; only authorized
Administrators provision or revoke Super User accounts.
System Capabilities
Shared Information and Automated Processing
Role-appropriate dashboards present relevant course, progress, task, coordination, or system
information. Shared records are retrieved through authorized backend workflows. The system
computes configured grades and progression values and produces permitted calendar outputs. In-
LMS updates and available platform-help functions follow the evaluated release; targeted event
visibility does not imply external-calendar synchronization or push delivery.
Technology Integration
Connected Applications and Data Services
The Next.js Web Portal and backend connect PostgreSQL records, the Expo/React Native
mobile client, and the Electron Administrator Console. Programming execution, repository
integration, file storage, and supported account-related email use their configured services. Final
versions, supported languages, client builds, and enabled services will be recorded in Chapter 3.

Security Features
Account and Information Protection
Credential authentication, account-status checks, and server-side authorization restrict access
by role, institute, ownership, enrollment, and related resources. Any verification or approval
requirements must agree with the evaluated workflow. Restricted supervision excludes student
identities, grades, submissions, attempts, and answers. Designated changes are audited; constraints,
transactions, and reviewed update rules protect record integrity. Repository authorization remains
separate from LMS login.
Unique or Innovative Features
ICS Workflow Integration
The project brings academic management, separate execution and repository coursework,
personal study, participation records, and moderated collaboration into an ICS-specific environment.
Complementary platform responsibilities and bounded academic oversight define its intended
configuration. The proposed calendar expansion connects faculty coordination and private
organization while preserving schedule history and information boundaries. These contributions will
be evaluated within ICS without claiming that comparable functions are absent from other LMS
products.

1.9 DEFINITION OF TERMS
Academic Calendar - The interface presenting authorized saved events, generated class occurrences,
and coursework deadlines through Day, Week, Month, and Year views.
Academic Operations Hub - The web interface through which a Super User views authorized
academic summaries, faculty information, timetable filters, and course-supervision links.
Administrator - The system role responsible for authorized account, permission, configuration, log,
reporting, and continuity operations through the native Administrator Console.
Agile Development - The iterative development approach in which requirements are implemented,
tested, reviewed, and refined through successive project cycles.
Audit Log - A record of designated actions and changes used to support accountability, including
authorized administrative and academic-leadership operations.
BSCpE - Bachelor of Science in Computer Engineering, one of the ICS programs within the study
context.
BSIT - Bachelor of Science in Information Technology, one of the ICS programs within the study
context.
CdM LMS - The proposed interconnected learning management environment developed for the
Institute of Computing Studies at Colegio de Montalban.
Centralized Database - The shared PostgreSQL data store supporting authorized academic and system
records used by the applicable applications.
CodeLab - The in-browser programming environment for writing, executing, and submitting code
assessed against predefined test cases.
Course Supervision - Restricted, read-only access to course metadata, instructor attribution,
timetable, announcements, syllabus, and learning-material summaries.
Dean - An academic leadership designation represented in the institute directory; the designation
itself does not grant additional system permissions.

Dynamic Gradebook - The grading module that uses configured components, weights, and recorded
scores to compute and display authorized grade information.
Effective Date - The date from which a particular timetable revision governs the generation of
applicable recurring class occurrences.
Experience Points or EXP - Configured participation points used for gamified progression and related
rewards; they are not equivalent to course grades or forum reputation.
Faculty Directory - The authorized listing of ICS faculty, program affiliations, leadership
designations, and relevant assigned-course summaries.
Faculty-Verified Answer - A Knowledge Exchange response marked by authorized faculty through
the platform’s answer-verification process.
Flashcard Review - Repeated study of saved question-and-answer cards using the review and mastery
functions available in the evaluated release.
Gamification - The use of configured points, levels, badges, achievements, streaks, and leaderboards
to support participation in permitted LMS activities.
Git-Integrated Submission Engine - The workflow for repository-based coursework submission and
authorized instructor review of applicable programming activities.
Institute of Computing Studies or ICS - The institute at Colegio de Montalban that defines the
development context and research-evaluation scope of the study.
Instructor - The system role responsible for authorized teaching, assessment, grading, and course-
related communication for assigned courses.
Knowledge Exchange - The moderated environment for academic and technical questions, answers,
and resource sharing, with faculty verification and reputation mechanisms.
Learning Management System or LMS - The application environment used in this study to organize
course resources, coursework, assessment, academic records, and related support workflows.

Program Head - An academic designation attached to an eligible ICS Instructor account for a
specified program, with defined coordination privileges.
Reputation Points - Configured points associated with Knowledge Exchange contributions,
maintained distinctly from EXP unless an explicit rule connects them.
Role-Based Access Control or RBAC - The mechanism that restricts system capabilities according
to assigned roles, supplemented by institute, ownership, enrollment, and related-resource checks.
Schedule Exception - A record modifying an individual class occurrence through cancellation or
rescheduling, or supporting restoration of its original occurrence.
Snapshot Conversion - Creation of a private note or calendar event from accessible source content at
the time of conversion, without continuous synchronization.
Student - The system role permitted to access enrolled-course content, submit assigned work, view
authorized personal academic records, and use available learning-support functions.
Super User - The system role for limited academic oversight and coordination, separate from
Instructor and Administrator privileges.
Targeted Event - A saved academic event whose visibility and management are governed by its
designated personal, course, institute-faculty, or program-instructor audience.
Timetable Revision - An effective-dated version of a course schedule used to preserve the historical
representation of recurring class times.
Visual Grade Analytics - Descriptive charts and summaries derived from available grade and
performance records, without predictive or AI-based inference.

CHAPTER 2: REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE
Digital technology has changed how educational institutions organize instruction and manage
academic information. Learning Management Systems (LMS) provide a shared environment for
distributing course materials, managing assignments, recording grades, and communicating with
students. Access through different devices also creates opportunities to connect classroom activities
with independent study. These functions provide the foundation for examining how an LMS can
support academic work within higher education.
In the Philippine context, the studies reviewed in this chapter examine LMS adoption, user
experience, accessibility, and institutional support. They also explore programming practice,
gamification, personal learning strategies, and online collaboration. Their findings provide different
perspectives on digital learning, including the difficulties users encounter and the conditions that
support meaningful participation. Understanding these findings helps guide the selection and
integration of functions appropriate to the Institute of Computing Studies (ICS) at Colegio de
Montalban.
The project developers reviewed scholarly articles, conference papers, and system-based
studies to establish the foundation for the proposed Learning Management System. Philippine and
international studies are organized under eight topic groups: Multi-Platform Learning Management
Systems; Course Management and Academic Communication; Programming Practice and
Automated Assessment; Git-Based Coursework Submission; Gamification and Student Engagement;
Personal Study Tools and Self-Regulated Learning; Online Collaboration and Knowledge Sharing;
and Academic Coordination and Information Boundaries. The discussion compares their findings,
explains their connection to the proposed system, and identifies the research gap that the study will
address.

2.1 Related Literature
2.1.1 Multi-Platform Learning Management Systems
Access through different devices should support useful academic tasks and an understandable
learning environment. Alfalah (2023) surveyed 258 students from Hail University, Aljouf University,
and Northern Border University in Saudi Arabia about mobile LMS adoption, including the
Blackboard application. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and learning intention were
associated with behavioral intention to use the system. In the Philippines, Dela Rosa (2023) examined
Canvas Free for Teachers with 132 third-year BSIT students taking Web Systems and Technologies
2 at Bulacan State University. Students evaluated its lesson modules and assessments favorably. Both
studies connect adoption with users' experiences of academic functions, although Alfalah examined
mobile-use intentions and Dela Rosa examined acceptance within a specific programming course.
Philippine development studies provide more direct examples of designing learning access
across devices. Quimod et al. (2023) developed e-Modyul, a mobile and web LMS for Technical-
Vocational-Livelihood education, and evaluated it with 10 teachers and 20 students. Its approach
supports accessing lessons and assessments through different operating systems. Ramos et al. (2024),
researchers associated with the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU), developed a
Filipinized LMS responsive to Filipino nursing educators and learners. Their design considered
connectivity limitations, multimodal learning materials, communication, and collaboration. These
studies share an emphasis on access, but e-Modyul focuses on device coverage, while the Filipinized
LMS emphasizes adaptation to its users and educational context.
Platform access also depends on the quality of everyday workflows. Llamas et al. (2025)
examined the Moodle-based LMS at Mindanao State University–Iligan Institute of Technology
(MSU–IIT), involving six academics and six fourth-year students. They identified concerns in
usability, communication, course building, monitoring and assessment, content management, and
technical support. Their findings qualify the favorable acceptance evidence from Dela Rosa:
providing an LMS does not remove all difficulties in using it.

Taken together, the reviewed studies support designing complementary interfaces around the
tasks and access conditions of the intended users. For CdM LMS, the web application will provide
the principal academic environment, the mobile application will support selected student and
instructor functions, and the desktop application will serve the Administrator. Multi-platform access
therefore concerns coordinated responsibilities and consistent shared records rather than identical
functionality on every device. The reviewed studies inform this arrangement, while its suitability for
ICS will require evaluation of the implemented applications.
2.1.2 Course Management and Academic Communication
Course management connects learning materials, activities, academic records, and
communication within a clear workflow. Peralta (2024) developed a course management system for
Centro Escolar University and evaluated it with 100 students and eight faculty members. It organized
materials, announcements, assignments, quizzes, and grades and included Short Messaging Service
notifications. Llamas et al. (2025), however, identified course-building, content-management,
communication, and assessment concerns in the MSU–IIT LMS. These studies suggest that
organizing functions within one platform is useful, but users must still be able to complete their tasks
without unnecessary difficulty.
The communication experience also varies across educational settings. Acala and Dimasacat
(2023) examined perceptions of 74 private senior high school students in Manila and reported
favorable views of LMS-supported interaction and learning. They recommended training to help
students and teachers use the available functions. Laspiñas and Almerez (2024), in contrast, surveyed
33 business graduate students at an unnamed university in Cebu City and reported generally neutral
evaluations of the LMS's pragmatic and hedonic qualities. Their findings address different
populations, yet both indicate that communication and task support should be assessed through users'
experiences rather than inferred from the presence of features.
Institutional support affects whether these workflows can be maintained. Guico (2026)
examined 182 faculty members and 29 administrators from 11 higher education institutions in

Batangas, including Batangas State University, Lipa City College, and Rizal College of Taal.
Reported concerns included preparation time, resistance to change, access to information and
communication technology resources, and continuing training. These findings place course
management within faculty support and institutional coordination.
Across the reviewed studies, effective academic communication depends on understandable
course organization, appropriate user preparation, and the support needed to sustain the system. This
evidence informs CdM's course materials, announcements, submissions, feedback, dynamic grading,
and descriptive grade analytics. It also supports considering faculty organization, schedules, and
targeted academic events as part of course coordination. Peralta's SMS function remains a comparison
feature of that system; the proposed CdM workflow uses its own documented notification functions.
Requirements gathering at ICS will establish the local difficulties to be addressed.
2.1.3 Programming Practice and Automated Assessment
Programming practice requires suitable exercises and feedback that explains performance
against clear criteria. Messer et al. (2024) reviewed 121 papers on automated grading and feedback
tools for programming education. Many tools evaluated correctness through dynamic methods such
as unit tests, while readability, maintainability, and documentation received less attention. Novak and
Kermek (2024), from the University of Zagreb in Croatia, examined automation for complex
programming assignments using unit testing and custom scripts. Both studies support automating
selected checks while retaining instructor judgment for aspects that those checks cannot adequately
assess.
Philippine research adds considerations about introductory practice and access. Asuncion et
al. (2022), affiliated with Ateneo de Manila University and the National Olympiad in Informatics–
Philippines, presented the ABC Workbook and AutoJudge++. The project combines introductory
Python exercises with an offline desktop checker that compares outputs against test cases. Classroom
effectiveness evaluation remained future work. Arada (2025) examined Tinkercad with 42 first-year
Computer Technology students at a Philippine state university. The platform received a below-

average System Usability Scale score of 58, despite many students expressing willingness to use it.
These studies concern different tools, but together they show that opportunities to practice should be
considered alongside exercise design, usability, and access conditions.
Assessment can also concern development processes beyond the output of an individual
program. Fernandez-Gauna et al. (2023), from the University of the Basque Country in Spain,
described automated feedback and assessment for team-coding assignments in a DevOps context.
Their approach used team and individual indicators and periodic reports to support monitoring.
Compared with the test-case approaches examined by Messer et al. and Asuncion et al., this work
illustrates a broader form of assessment involving collaborative development activity. It does not
establish that development indicators can replace assessment of the submitted program.
The reviewed studies support matching automated feedback to the assignment and preserving
the limits of what is measured. CdM's CodeLab will evaluate programming work against predefined
test cases and provide understandable results. Its checks will concern documented expected behavior
rather than complete program quality. Git-based coursework review will remain a separate workflow.
The related studies therefore guide test design, feedback presentation, and usability without
expanding CodeLab into automated code repair, artificial intelligence grading, or DevOps-based team
assessment.
2.1.4 Git-Based Coursework Submission
Repository-based coursework can connect code submissions with an organized record of
development and instructor review. Schauer et al. (2024), from Heriot-Watt University in the United
Kingdom, developed a framework integrating Canvas LMS and GitLab. They identified fragmented
information and poor user experiences when the platforms were used independently and implemented
eight applications to connect their workflows. Orvalho et al. (2024), affiliated with the University of
Lisbon and Czech Technical University in Prague, presented GitSEED, a GitLab-backed automated
assessment tool. Both approaches connect academic work with version control, although Schauer et

al. emphasize LMS integration and GitSEED provides assessment and feedback through repository
workflows.
Evidence about students' use of repositories complements these system-development
approaches. Patani et al. (2024) examined GitHub use in a software engineering course with 319
undergraduate students, using surveys and repository records such as commits, pull requests, and
issues. They reported improvements in collaborative development and teamwork after the course
experience. Fernandez-Gauna et al. (2023) used repository-related development indicators to provide
feedback on team-coding assignments. Together, these studies show how repositories can make
development activity available for educational review, but their measures extend beyond recording a
final coursework submission.
The reviewed studies support examining how academic instructions, repository records, and
instructor feedback can be connected. For CdM LMS, Git authorization will support the documented
repository submission and review process, while LMS account access will follow its separate
authentication and approval rules. Repository submissions will not automatically become CodeLab
assessments or commit-based academic grades. The project's contribution is to evaluate its particular
coursework workflow for ICS, informed by the integration concerns identified by Schauer et al. and
the educational repository use described in the other studies.
2.1.5 Gamification and Student Engagement
Gamification can encourage participation when rewards are connected to meaningful learning
activities. Ahmed et al. (2025) evaluated a gamified, mobile, cloud-based LMS with 60 second-year
students taking Object-Oriented Programming at Mansoura University in Egypt. The experimental
group obtained higher post-test achievement and engagement scores than the comparison group.
Jaramillo-Mediavilla et al. (2024) synthesized gamification research and reported favorable findings
in parts of the literature while identifying gaps in examining motivation and academic performance
together. These studies support investigating gamification, but the outcomes of a particular
intervention should not be treated as a guaranteed effect of every reward system.

The design of participation incentives matters. Jack (2025), in a conference abstract, discussed
points and leaderboards in a flipped statistics classroom and considered benefits for motivation and
engagement alongside the risks of superficial engagement and demotivation. Philippine evidence
from Fojas (2022) examined gamification in Moodle courses at UPOU, comparing a gamified cohort
with earlier non-gamified cohorts and collecting student feedback. The reported differences favored
the gamified course, but forum-grading arrangements also differed between cohorts, and some
students described anxiety or limited interest in rewards. Both studies show why participation counts
and positive feedback need to be interpreted in relation to the design of the activities.
Benben and Bug-os (2022) studied Quizizz-based formative assessment with Grade 10
physics students at Central Mindanao University Laboratory High School in Bukidnon. Achievement
and motivation increased after the intervention, although the reported learning gain was low. Its one-
group pretest-posttest design and secondary-school setting differ from Ahmed et al.'s computing-
course comparison. The studies therefore provide complementary evidence about possible
motivational benefits while leaving questions about transfer to other subjects and populations.
Across the reviewed studies, gamification is most relevant when its rules encourage
participation without obscuring academic expectations. CdM LMS will use EXP, levels,
achievements, streaks, and leaderboards under defined rules. These records will remain separate from
academic grades and Knowledge Exchange reputation. The literature supports the rationale for these
mechanisms and the need to examine users' experiences, while the proposed descriptive software-
quality evaluation will not establish their long-term causal effects on achievement or motivation.
2.1.6 Personal Study Tools and Self-Regulated Learning
Personal study tools can support planning, active review, and reflection when learners use
them purposefully. Du et al. (2025) examined an LMS enhanced with self-regulated learning support
among 69 management undergraduates taking mathematics at an unnamed large public university in
China. Students reported stronger self-regulation, but an examination advantage appeared on the first
test and not the second. Heikkinen et al. (2023), in a review of 56 studies, found that only 46 percent

of the reviewed learning-analytics interventions reported positive effects on learning. Both studies
indicate that learning support deserves investigation, while access to monitoring tools alone does not
ensure improved outcomes.
Students' interactions with LMS tools help explain differences in how learning support is
used. Çakiroğlu et al. (2024) examined a third-year Operating Systems and Applications course at an
unnamed public university in Turkey. They identified different learner profiles and relationships
between assessment interactions and self-regulation skills, including goal setting, self-evaluation, and
help-seeking. In the Philippines, Funa et al. (2023) surveyed 301 preservice teachers in the Bicol
region and supplemented the survey with interviews. Participants reported relatively strong
environment structuring and goal setting but also difficulties with task strategies, time allocation,
priorities, and interaction. These studies connect self-regulation with both individual learning
practices and the conditions in which academic tasks are completed.
Active review provides another form of personal learning support. Pan et al. (2022) compared
user-generated and premade digital flashcards in six experiments involving delayed tests. Creating
flashcard content generally supported memory and, in several conditions, application performance.
Unlike the broader LMS and analytics studies, this research examines a specific review activity. It
offers a direct basis for considering student-created flashcards alongside the organization and
reflection functions discussed by Du et al., Çakiroğlu et al., and Funa et al.
Together, the reviewed studies support making planning, review, and progress information
available within the learning environment. For CdM LMS, personal notes, tasks, flashcards, review
and mastery records, and focus-study records will provide ways to organize and revisit academic
work. Descriptive displays can help users inspect their saved records, but their presence will not be
treated as evidence of improved self-regulation. The implemented functions will require evaluation
for usability and correct behavior, while their educational effects remain a possible direction for later
research.

2.1.7 Online Collaboration and Knowledge Sharing
Online knowledge sharing depends on the quality of interaction and the way discussions are
organized. Oyarzun and Martin (2023) reviewed 63 studies on online learner collaboration and
examined technologies, instructional design, facilitation, and outcomes. Their review connects
collaboration with the conditions supporting participation. Bach and Thiel (2024) surveyed 298
undergraduate teacher-education students in asynchronous university courses and examined
cognitive, metacognitive, and relational dimensions of interaction. Their findings concern
associations with self-reported learning gains and satisfaction rather than causal effects. Both studies
indicate that a shared online space should be assessed through the exchanges it supports.
Structured discussions and instructor involvement provide more specific guidance. Mudau
and Van den Berg (2023), from the University of South Africa, examined online discussions
involving 11 master's students in education. They identified the importance of clear guidelines,
structured questions, and opportunities for discussion within a community of inquiry. Almodiel
(2022) analyzed knowledge construction in asynchronous discussions within a graduate colloquium
at UPOU. The study used the Interaction Analysis Model to examine the exchanges through which
learners shared and developed knowledge. These studies support considering discussion structure and
facilitation alongside opportunities for students to contribute.
Participation measures should also reflect interaction between users. Kumi (2023) examined
discussion-forum exchanges in an undergraduate class with 31 students using social network analysis.
The analysis revealed structural and relational aspects of participation that simple counts or self-
reports could overlook. This complements Almodiel's examination of knowledge construction: both
approaches look beyond the number of messages to consider how students interact. Their analytical
methods are research approaches rather than functions automatically required in the proposed CdM
system.
The reviewed studies support designing Knowledge Exchange as an organized space for
academic questions, answers, and resource sharing. Moderation and Faculty-Verified Answers will

provide project-specific ways to manage contributions and identify instructor-reviewed responses.
Reputation will describe forum participation under its configured rules and remain separate from EXP
and academic grades. The literature provides reasons to examine participation, facilitation, and
contribution quality, while the suitability of CdM's verification and reputation mechanisms will
require its own evaluation. The proposed forum supports asynchronous exchanges; the reviewed
studies do not require adding live meetings or collaborative document editing.
2.1.8 Academic Coordination and Information Boundaries
Institutional LMS support extends beyond individual coursework. Guico (2026) identifies
faculty preparation, resource access, and continuing training as management concerns. Llamas et al.
(2025) identify monitoring, assessment, communication, and course organization as user-experience
concerns. Together, these findings provide reasons to examine faculty coordination and access to
appropriate course information. They do not validate the particular schedule schema or supervision
policy proposed for CdM LMS.
The project’s academic coordination requirements will therefore be established through local
consultation and explicit role policies. Directory information, timetable revisions, event audiences,
and restricted supervision will be tested against those requirements. Academic designation and
technical privilege will remain separate; shared calendar visibility will not imply access to private
notes or individual assessment records.
2.2 Supporting Quality Framework and Local Study Context
ISO/IEC 25010:2023 provides the product-quality model supporting the study's selected
evaluation characteristics: functional suitability, interaction capability, security, performance
efficiency, reliability, and compatibility (International Organization for Standardization, 2023). The
standard supports the quality criteria used in this study. Questionnaire feedback will describe
respondents' evaluations, while calculation checks, access tests, and integration verification will
provide evidence about implemented behavior.

The reviewed Philippine studies inform the project’s computing-course, LMS, programming,
and collaborative workflows. Their findings do not establish conditions within ICS. Local
requirements gathering will identify the needs and experiences of the intended users.
2.3 Related Systems
The following systems provide documented examples of course organization, progress
information, and repository-based workflows. The comparison uses the capabilities described in the
cited sources rather than an exhaustive feature audit. It does not assume that these platforms lack
other functions or cannot be extended.
2.3.1 Moodle
Moodle's publication on LMS 4.5 described improvements to assignment interaction and
course subsections for organizing content (Moodle, 2024). Llamas et al. (2025) examined its
institutional use at MSU–IIT, while Fojas (2022) and Almodiel (2022) examined gamification and
discussions in the UPOU context. These sources show that Moodle can support several forms of
academic work. For CdM LMS, the relevant comparison concerns the organization of coursework
and the experience of completing institutional tasks.
2.3.2 Google Classroom
Mennuti (2024) described targeted assignments, rubrics, and analytics for grades, completion
rates, and missing work in Google Classroom. The analytics described were associated with specified
education editions or upgrades. These functions provide comparison points for assignment
management and descriptive progress information. Their documentation does not establish the quality
of the proposed CdM implementation or demonstrate that it will outperform Classroom.
2.3.3 Canvas and GitLab Integration
Schauer et al. (2024) implemented a framework connecting Canvas and GitLab to reduce
fragmented workflows and support feedback. Its eight applications demonstrate that existing LMS
and version-control platforms can be connected for educational use. This is a direct comparison for

the integration concern in CdM's Git submission workflow. The technologies and automation
described in that framework remain distinct from CdM's specified implementation.
2.3.4 GitSEED
Orvalho et al. (2024) presented GitSEED as a GitLab-backed automated assessment tool
supporting programming and software engineering education. It uses repositories as part of
submission and feedback workflows. Its approach provides a comparison for connecting coursework
with version control, but its automated assessment capabilities extend beyond CdM's separate
repository-submission and instructor-review process.
2.4 Synthesis of the Literature
The literature connects LMS adoption with useful academic functions, understandable
interaction, and conditions supporting continued use. Alfalah (2023) and Dela Rosa (2023) address
acceptance, while Quimod et al. (2023), Ramos et al. (2024), and Llamas et al. (2025) provide
development and user-experience perspectives. Peralta (2024), Guico (2026) further connect
coursework with communication and institutional support. These studies support examining
connected workflows and appropriate access across CdM's complementary applications.
Programming and repository research address related but distinct academic processes. Messer
et al. (2024), Asuncion et al. (2022), and Novak and Kermek (2024) inform checks against specified
programming criteria. Schauer et al. (2024), Orvalho et al. (2024), and Patani et al. (2024) inform
repository use and integration. The comparison supports keeping CodeLab's test-case assessment
separate from Git-based coursework review, with instructors retaining responsibility for judgments
outside the automated checks.
Gamification, personal study support, and collaboration concern different aspects of
participation. Ahmed et al. (2025), Jack (2025), and Fojas (2022) provide evidence about rewards
and engagement. Du et al. (2025), Heikkinen et al. (2023), Funa et al. (2023), and Pan et al. (2022)
address regulation and active review. Oyarzun and Martin (2023), Almodiel (2022), and Mudau and

Van den Berg (2023) emphasize interaction and facilitation. Their combined implication is to provide
learning support with clear purposes and evaluate how the intended users experience it.
For the present study, these findings inform the development and descriptive evaluation of an
LMS configured for ICS. Evidence from other institutions provides design guidance and comparison
points. The study will establish its own findings about software quality and workflow suitability,
while recognizing that user ratings and functional verification do not establish long-term educational
effects.
2.5 Research Gap
The reviewed studies address digital learning and institutional LMS utilization but do not
evaluate the proposed CdM LMS configuration for ICS at Colegio de Montalban. The research gap
is contextual and evaluative: evidence is needed about how its combined workflows, roles, and
complementary applications operate in the intended setting. One part of the gap concerns functional
integration. CdM LMS will combine routine academic management with separate CodeLab and Git-
submission workflows, learning-support tools, and moderated collaboration. Its evaluation must
determine whether the selected functions produce the expected results and interact consistently within
a shared information environment. This is a system-specific question; it is not a claim that no existing
platform can provide similar integration.
A second part concerns academic coordination and information boundaries. The proposed
expansion introduces an academic Super User, restricted course supervision, faculty organization,
effective-dated timetable revisions, class exceptions, and audience-targeted events. The reviewed
literature provides organizational reasons to consider coordination, but it does not establish whether
CdM’s particular implementation preserves schedule behavior, correct audiences, and restricted
information access. These properties require requirements-based testing and evaluation of the
implemented release.
A third part concerns role-appropriate access across applications. The web environment,
complementary mobile client, and native Administrator Console have distinct responsibilities. The

study will examine consistency in their applicable shared records and the quality of the tasks each
interface supports, without assuming universal feature parity. Findings will identify the suitability
and limitations of this configuration for ICS. The study will address these gaps through development,
documented verification, and descriptive software-quality evaluation, producing evidence about the
suitability and limitations of the ICS implementation.

CHAPTER 3: METHODOLOGY
3.1 RESEARCH DESIGN
The study will combine iterative system development, requirements-based technical
verification, and quantitative descriptive evaluation. Descriptive research systematically
characterizes observed conditions and experiences without establishing causal effects (McCombes,
2023). Questionnaires will describe users’ experiences with assigned tasks; controlled technical
checks will examine correctness, access restrictions, record handling, performance, and integration.
The two evidence types will be reported separately and considered together.
The Agile operational framework in Section 1.5 will guide development. Chapter 3 specifies
how local requirements, evaluation participants, instruments, tests, and analysis will be organized.
The evaluation will address six selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics rather than claim
assessment of the complete standard or ISO certification.
3.2 SYSTEM AND PROJECT OVERVIEW
CdM LMS connects the principal Web Portal, complementary Expo/React Native application,
and native Electron Administrator Console to Next.js backend workflows and PostgreSQL records.
Students access approved coursework and their own academic and study information. Instructors
manage assigned teaching activities. Super Users perform restricted academic coordination through
the web; Administrators operate the native console. Program Head and Dean designations remain
separate from those account roles.
The evaluation configuration will identify enabled modules, client builds, roles, and datasets.
Existing functions and proposed coordination extensions will have separate implementation and test-
status entries. Only demonstrated functions will be included in respondent tasks and reported as
evaluated.

3.3 RESPONDENTS
The respondents will consist only of selected ICS students and instructors at Colegio de
Montalban. Student respondents must be officially enrolled in the BSIT or BSCpE program, have
previous experience using at least one LMS, voluntarily agree to participate, and complete the
assigned evaluation tasks. Participation will not be restricted to a single year level. Their tasks will
cover approved coursework, learning resources, submissions, personal grades, study tools, and
Knowledge Exchange functions available in the evaluated release.
Instructor respondents must currently teach BSIT or BSCpE courses within ICS, have prior
LMS experience relevant to their academic responsibilities, voluntarily participate, and complete the
assigned tasks. They will evaluate course management, assessment, submissions, grading, enrollment
decisions, communication, and applicable calendar functions. Instructors holding a Program Head
designation may evaluate its permitted coordination functions. That designation does not grant Super
User or Administrator authority.
The capstone adviser and the three proposed faculty validators will review questionnaire
content separately from the respondent sample. Their review will not automatically make them
respondents; they may participate only if they independently satisfy the Instructor criteria. The
researchers will conduct technical verification of restricted supervision and native console functions
using controlled test accounts. There will be no IT-expert respondent group or separate expert
questionnaire.
Target numbers for Student and Instructor respondents will be finalized after confirming the
eligible population and feasible task sessions with the adviser. The researchers will report the invited,
participating, and valid responding counts separately for the two groups. No target or completed
sample count is asserted before that decision and data collection.
3.4 SAMPLING TECHNIQUE
The study will use criterion-based purposive sampling, a non-probability method in which
participants are selected according to requirements relevant to the study. Memon et al. (2025)

emphasize explicit, justified criteria for quantitative purposive sampling. This method is appropriate
because Students and Instructors must directly use the functions they will assess. Enrollment or
employment at the institution alone will not qualify a participant to rate every platform or system
function.
The researchers will screen the Student and Instructor criteria specified in Section 3.3, obtain
voluntary consent, and arrange orientation and task sessions through an approved recruitment
process. The invitation will explain the purpose, activities, participation conditions, and data use.
Sample justification will consider coverage of the two programs, eligible year levels, teaching
responsibilities, enabled functions, and feasible evaluation arrangements. Participation and
nonresponse will be recorded by group.
Students will assess permitted academic and study functions, while Instructors will assess
teaching and course-management workflows. Participants will not receive elevated roles merely to
complete the questionnaire. Findings will describe the selected respondents and evaluated release
within ICS; purposive selection will not be presented as a probability sample representing the entire
student or instructor population.
3.5 INSTRUMENTS AND METHODS FOR DATA COLLECTION
3.5.1 Questionnaires and Instrument Review
Survey questionnaires will be the primary instruments for collecting quantitative user
feedback. Two role-specific forms will be prepared: a Student questionnaire and an Instructor
questionnaire. Both will align with the six selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics: functional
suitability, interaction capability, security, performance efficiency, reliability, and compatibility.
Items will describe one observable behavior and identify the relevant task. Students and Instructors
will rate only functions they have directly used; restricted console or supervision operations will not
appear as ordinary user-survey tasks.

Both forms will use Strongly Agree (4), Agree (3), Disagree (2), and Strongly Disagree (1).
A separate “Not applicable or not observed” option will receive no numerical score. Security items
for respondents will concern observable access boundaries and protection of their own records;
resource utilization, prohibited requests, and other internal properties will be examined through the
researchers’ technical tests. The survey will not be represented as proof of all technical
subcharacteristics.
Before administration, the capstone adviser and three proposed faculty validators from
Colegio de Montalban will review clarity, relevance, alignment with the research questions, and
suitability for each role. The researchers will revise the instruments and conduct a pilot with eligible
Students and Instructors outside the main sample. Reviewer approval will support content review;
any internal-consistency assessment will use actual pilot responses and an appropriate analysis rather
than infer reliability from approval alone.
Participants will receive orientation and consent information, perform the documented task
sequence using authorized accounts, and then complete the applicable questionnaire. The researchers
will record respondent group, platform and client build, task completion, and encountered difficulties.
Local requirements consultations will precede final development and will remain separate from the
post-development evaluation survey.

3.5.2 Local Requirements Gathering
Before finalizing the development backlog, the researchers will seek institutional permission
to gather local requirements from ICS students and instructors through guided interviews or small-

group consultations and available workflow descriptions. Topics will cover resource distribution,
enrollment, submissions, grading, programming coursework, personal organization, faculty

3.5.3 Technical Testing and Observation
A test matrix will map requirements to selected quality characteristics, account roles,
platforms, datasets, and expected outcomes. Each case will record the application revision, enabled
feature, setup, action, result, error evidence, and retest status. Calculation checks will compare
outputs with manually verified expected records. Security cases will invoke prohibited reads/writes
directly rather than rely on hidden interface buttons.
The researchers will define workload and dataset sizes before performance testing. Logged-

Reliability checks will examine saved records after refresh, interrupted requests, retries,
duplicate conversion, stale saves, and relevant concurrent updates. Researcher-conducted
compatibility checks will verify shared records through permitted clients and observe the

will use an isolated database. Unexecuted or failed cases will remain visible in the evaluation record;
fresh evidence will support any reported pass.

3.5.4 Data Analysis and Statistical Treatment
Questionnaire responses will be tabulated by respondent group, item, and quality
characteristic. Frequencies and percentages will describe response distributions. The valid count for
each item will exclude unanswered and Not applicable or not observed responses; those exclusions
will also be reported. N/A will not be treated as zero, disagreement, or a passing result.
For comparability with the coded scale, an item mean will be calculated as the sum of valid
response scores divided by the valid response count. Equivalently, the frequency-weighted mean is
(4f4 + 3f3 + 2f2 + f1) / (f4 + f3 + f2 + f1). Frequency weighting represents counts of responses, not
different importance weights for users or quality characteristics. Response distributions and valid
counts will accompany means; median summaries may be reported to retain visibility of the ordered
categories.
Characteristic summaries will first be computed for each respondent from the applicable
items, then summarized within the Student or Instructor group. The number of applicable items and
contributing respondents will be reported. Results from different roles or questionnaire versions will
not be pooled into one score unless item equivalence and weighting are explicitly justified. Numeric
results will be reported on the 1–4 scale without unapproved labels such as highly acceptable.

Technical results will be reported by test case and characteristic. Correctness and access cases
will identify expected/actual outcomes and pass, fail, or not executed status. Timings will identify
workload, repetitions, median and observed slow cases; resource observations will identify the
measurement conditions. Favorable questionnaire means will not override failed authorization,
calculation, or persistence tests. The study will use descriptive summaries and will not claim causal
educational effects or population-wide statistical representation.
3.5.5 Participant Protection and Information Handling
The researchers will obtain applicable institutional permission before recruitment or access to
restricted records. Participants will receive information about purpose, tasks, duration, data use, and
voluntary participation. Declining or withdrawing will not affect grades, employment, or access to
ordinary institutional services. Consent will be obtained before task participation and questionnaire
collection.
Evaluation identifiers will replace participant names in analysis files. The researchers will use
controlled accounts and synthetic or appropriately de-identified academic records for restricted tests.
Only authorized members of the research team and approved reviewers will access identifiable
materials. Storage location, access controls, retention period, and deletion arrangements will be
specified in the approved protocol. Public reports will present aggregate results and avoid exposing
credentials, repository tokens, or personal academic records.
3.5.6 Evaluation Release Record
Before recruitment, the researchers will record the application revision, client builds, schema
and migration state, enabled modules and languages, repository provider, file limits, device/browser
matrix, network conditions, role accounts, datasets, and known limitations. Existing modules,
planned extensions, tested functions, and functions enabled for respondent tasks will be identified
separately. Administrator and Super User functions will be verified by the researchers with controlled
accounts; ordinary respondents will not rate functions outside their authority. Secrets and identifiable
academic records will be excluded from manuscript examples.
